narrative: The model estimated an 82% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this is a high failure risk, your law school application was rejected. The strongest driver was your third-year class standing: you were in decile 1, while accepted students averaged around decile 6. This was the most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second-most influential factor: at 22.50, it is well below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third-most influential factor. At 2.70 it is below the accepted average of 3.23, but in your case this factor pushed toward passing, slightly offsetting the other two signals rather than causing the denial. To improve future chances, focus on what you can change. Retake the LSAT after structured preparation, since a stronger score would directly address one of the main failure signals. Seek academic advising and consider additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates readiness for law study; also ask admissions whether an appeal or feedback process exists. Reapply only after you can show stronger standardized-test performance and evidence that your academic trajectory has improved, and include schools where your revised profile fits their admitted-student range.
